newsitem.title: NORTH KOREA: North Korean meet draws $282 mln in foreign investment.
newsitem.headline: North Korean meet draws $282 mln in foreign investment.

text.p: Reclusive North Korea's biggest experiment with capitalism bore its first fruit on Sunday as foreign businessmen clinched $282 million in deals with the isolated Stalinist state.

In addition to the agreements, which ranged from hotels to motorcycle plants, foreign executives initialed letters of understanding to explore other deals worth $840 million, North Korean officials said at the end of the historic forum.

North Korea, which has sneered at the capitalist world for decades, is hoping to create a 750 sq km (280 sq mile) free trade zone in its northeast and attract enough foreign investors to help revive its teetering economy.

But North Korea's new-found pragmatism was mixed with its customary hard-line politics as its officials used a news conference at the forum's close to blast rival South Korea, which boycotted the forum after Pyongyang refused to invite some of its proposed delegates.

"I believe South Korea played political games with the forum -- out of 140 businessmen we invited, they chose only 24 that they planned to allow to visit our country," said Kim Jong-u, chairman of the Committee for Promotion of External Economic Cooperation.
"We cannot hold any dialogue as long as the present government is in power in South Korea, but dialogue between businessmen is another matter," Kim said.

Confirmed deals included a $180 million plan by the Emperor Group of Hong Kong to build a five-star hotel and casino on the coast near Rajin. The group would invest an additional $30 million in a banking venture, a North Korean official said.

An overseas Korean conglomerate headed by Japan-based Kim Man-ju, committed $50 million to build a hospital and China's Yantai Motorcycle Co will build a $5 million motorcycle plant in the special zone, the official said.

Thailand's Loxley Group agreed to invest $10 million in a project to build prefabricated housing and upgrade telecommunications system in Rajin-Sonbong located in the northeast corner of North Korea near the Chinese border.
Observers at the forum said negotiations for a joint venture flour mill with the bordering Chinese province of Yangi and talks for an oil refinery were also likely to yield deals.
Yangi province was also said to be discussing a deal for a bottling plant and an plastic factory.
"There are definitely things happening here, it's just a matter of what people do after the forum rather than what they say here," said an economic researcher from the United States.

North Korea's first attempt at linking up with capitalism has attracted 550 businessmen and reporters who joined North Korean officials for seminars on tourism, banking, agriculture, electronics manufacturing and infrastructure development.
North Korea, eager to impress its guests, built a gleaming new conference centre in the middle of the free trade zone on the Tumen River border region with China and Russia.

North Korean officials quickly got down to business. With the paint still wet on the new building, trade oficial Kim Jong-u appealed for billions of dollars of investment in what he depicted as a free trade zone with low taxes, visa-free travel, high-tech infrastructure and laws governing investment.

The omnipresent "guides" shadowing guests eventually relaxed enough to allow foreigners to walk freely in Rajin and Sonbong cities. Businessmen were seen wandering into residential neighborhoods, much to the surprise of residents.
Outside urban areas, Rajin-Songong appeared desolate, with only one village visible on the 50 km (30 mile) drive to the Chinese border to the north.

During the hour-long trip, visitors saw only two cargo trucks on the road which carries goods from Rajin Sonbong to Yangi Province. The goods originate in Pusan, South Korea, with which North Korea is still technically at war, and are brought to Ragjin Sonbong by boat.
Western business men were few in the mostly Asian group, and United States executives -- barred by U.S. law from trading with North Korea -- could be counted on one hand.
"We can talk but we can't do business. At some point we hope to get some kind of approval," said Donald Abresch, representative director of Monsanto Co in South Korea.
"At this point we're here to listen and learn," he said.
